text:
AI is useful outside of the narrative process.

My approach is to use LLMs when I'm researching an idea (it's simply more efficient than Google and links to sources).

Once I'm confident enough to speak to the topic, I do so literally, using Whisper to transcribe.

Then I have the LLM insert that into my blog, with explicit instructions to not alter any of the transcribed text, because preserving my own voice is mission critical.

Then I editorialize the prose manually, making any verbal-only phrasing make sense in a written context.

Finally, I prompt several LLMs to function as a panel, trying to surface anything objectionable or outright false in my post (I'm human so I make mistakes and want to be aware of them).  If anything salient is in the notes, I'll manually adjust my post.

Point is LLMs are used fortuitously, and you don't need to let their prose bleed into the text.

I can see how it could be useful as a language translation layer, especially since romantic and germanic languages are so idiomatic.

text:
I tried something like this myself, especially on the translation front, and concluded that LLMs are woefully not up to the task. Perhaps French is easier for LLMs to handle and produce satisfactory results than Polish, but the blog posts that I translated using Claude Opus from English to Polish are just... terrible, honestly.

I suspect part of it is in the nature of how autoregressive LLMs operate. In Polish sometimes what you put at the end of the sentence can change the declension of what comes before, which is not the case in English. So if the model, in the process of generating a sentence, doesn't "know" whether it'll have a masculine or feminine subject at the end of the sentence, it will put incorrect endings on preceding words.

So at the end of the day I only have a few articles translated to Polish, because the price of a competent translator is not really justifiable for an independent blog, and I am hopeless at context switching so I can't do it myself properly without expending a lot of effort that could be better spent on original content.

In this article the section about the keyboard, and especially the four paragraphs starting with "In theory this works great..." (in Polish: "W teorii działa to świetnie...").

I ran it through Claude Opus without any additional prompting and the result again wasn't that great. Some of the more interesting choices that I disagree with:


Using "wpm" as the unit verbatim without explaining it.

Translating "chords" to "akordy," which is only really valid when talking about musical chords. (My choice was "zbitki," i.e. "clusters.")

Translating "common sequences of two letters" literally as "popularne sekwencje dwóch liter." The word "bigram" in English is relatively uncommon and technical, whereas the corresponding Polish word "dwuznak" is known to almost everyone because of the prevalence of orthographic bigrams in Polish it is learned as early as primary school.

"according to the classic home row method" was also translated literally "zgodnie z klasyczną metodą rzędu podstawowego (home row)." This sounds very clunky because while "home row method" is recognised as a term among English typists, I'm not aware of this being the case in Polish, and there is no direct recognised equivalent of "home row" in Polish. My choice here was "zgodnie z klasyczną szkołą pisania bezwzrokowego" ("according to the classic school of touch typing").

"That takes a long time, so fast typists use a technique called 'alternative fingering'" was rendered as "Zajmuje to dużo czasu, więc szybcy maszyniści stosują technikę zwaną «alternatywnym palcowaniem»." Two choices that I would consider wrong here. Firstly, the term "maszynist(k)a" for "typist" is very dated, having fallen out of use when typist stopped being a profession (it is also a homonym, "maszynista" also means "train engine driver"). The sentence flows in English, but in Polish had to be rewritten entirely. Secondly, "alternatywne palcowanie" sounds horrible, but I couldn't find a better Polish alternative so left it as an English term in scare quotes.

"There have been some attempts" as "Podejmowano pewne próby," the word "pewne" is entirely unnecessary in the Polish translation.

"for typists that use the home row method" again as "u maszynistów korzystających z metody rzędu podstawowego" - this is a good example where the DeepL style interface would be quite a lot better, because if I had specified earlier that I don't like this word choice it would most likely not generate this sentence at all in this form after the change was made once already. (My choice: "dla osób piszących na klawiaturze metodą klasyczną").

"struggling" as "męczarni" - much too strong of a word here, "męczarnia" is more like "torture," I went with "zmagań."

"I sold the Cheapino on Facebook Marketplace" - this was an interesting point of localisation, because I hadn't actually sold it on Facebook Marketplace, but on OLX. However, OLX is likely entirely unknown in the US and UK, where these kinds of sales happen on platforms like Facebook Marketplace or Craigslist, so instead of relating the name of the platform exactly (which was frankly irrelevant to the discussion) and adding a margin note explaining to the international audience what it is, I used the platform that's most likely to be known to users worldwide. In the Polish version I stuck to the actual events and mentioned selling it on OLX.

"row stagger, split and arrow keys" as "przesunięcia rzędowego, klawiatury dzielonej i klawiszy strzałek" - an accurate literal translation, but my own choice was a bit different. I avoided "row stagger" up to this point, generally speaking around it descriptively, so I chose "rozłożenia wierszy." "Split" on the other hand works perfectly as an anglicism (we usually adopt anglicisms when they fit Polish phonetics and "split" is pronounced almost exactly the same in English as in Polish), so I never used the term "klawiatura dzielona," instead opting for "klawiatura split."

"It came in barebones for quite cheap" as "Przyszła w wersji barebones, dość tanio." Apart from not matching the gender (the previous sentence refers to a "model" which is masculine, whereas here the verb is conjugated for a feminine noun, I suppose "klawiatura"/"keyboard"), the word "barebones" is unlikely to be understood as a technical term for anyone not into keyboards, so I chose to also add an explanation of what this means: "Był dostępny w wersji “barebones”, bez przełączników i klawiszy za dość niską cenę."


So, you know. That's quite a lot of issues in four paragraphs of content. The problem is that if I went into this blind and just took the output and converted individual parts, it's quite likely the overall quality of the translation would be much lower, because there wouldn't be the thinking involved around how to structure the entire essay, which terms to translate, which terms to leave as anglicisms, and which to speak around.

Good code is code that is easy to understand, navigate, extend, and delete.  To a certain extent these are aesthetic, subjective qualities, but they're also qualities that can be measured.  In the same way that we can talk about objective UX qualities of a particular design (acknowledging that that design will also always be a subjective experience), we could talk about the objective UX qualities of a particular implementation (acknowledging that many details of the implementation are entirely subjective).

Unfortunately, there's a huge dearth of high-quality research on what good code actually looks like, which is why most people perceive it as mainly a subjective thing.  There are some different attempts to try and define good code, and I think most experienced developers grow a kind of intuition for it, but the field is still very much in its infancy.

My own experience is that LLMs produce poor-to-mediocre code, at least by my own standards.  That is, the code they produce works, but is usually more complicated than it needs to be, and LLMs struggle to simplify code down.  When fixing things, they mostly fix by adding new code rather than fixing by deleting or cleaning up old code.  They can do very basic refactorings like factoring shared code out, but they can't make higher-level decisions about how to structure modules.  They remind me a lot of Uncle Bob's refactoring process: each individual step kind of makes sense, the end result, however, is insanity.

And I don't think that's going to improve, because, like I said, we don't really have clear answers about what good code looks like.  We don't have good measures of navigability or extensibility, and without objective measures, it's difficult to train the underlying models.

That said, how much is good code really worth?  Like I said, good code is quick to understand, navigate, extend, and delete.  When you onboard a new developer into a codebase, those qualities are all very important — they reduce how long it takes that developer to figure out what's going on and be able to make their own changes.  But LLMs can churn through mountains of code far quicker than a human can.  And while good code can also make LLMs quicker (at least in my experience), the amount of time that it saves is far less than the amount of time that it takes to convince an LLM to write good code.

I agree to an extent with the idea that LLMs enable a kind of higher-level approach, where the developer can think about the overall goals of the code, and the LLM can worry about the details of what variables get named or how function calls get broken up into parts.  But to a certain extent that makes me sad, because one of the things I found most interesting about programming was this question of how to write good code, and now it feels like that's just not a relevant question any more.

I like to think about shipping better code in terms of technical debt. We take on technical debt as the result of trade-offs: doing things "the right way" would take too long, so we work within the time constraints we are under and cross our fingers that our project will survive long enough to pay down the debt later on. ... In my experience, a common category of technical debt fixes is changes that are simple but time-consuming.


I want to call out that the reason "the right way" is time consuming is not because of the time it takes to generate the code. It's because managing the risk involved requires building scaffolding between the old and the new way, ensuring adequate test coverage and monitoring of that scaffolding, confirming through human code review that the outcomes meet our expectations, and then dealing with multiple deploys to cross the gap.

AIs might be able to help with the scaffolding and test coverage, but again generating those things is not the time consuming part. In all the companies I've worked at, refactoring takes time because you can't yeet code into production as fast as you can write it (and with good reason).


Any software development task comes with a wealth of options for approaching the problem. Some of the most significant technical debt comes from making poor choices at the planning step - missing out on an obvious simple solution, or picking a technology that later turns out not to be exactly the right fit.


I agree that most technical debt stems from poor choices during system design, but I disagree that it's due to missing out on obvious solutions or picking the wrong technology. The "official" definition of laziness from Wall's book:


The quality that makes you go to great effort to reduce overall energy expenditure. It makes you write labor-saving programs that other people will find useful, and document what you wrote so you don't have to answer so many questions about it.


How that applies to coding-without-thinking (misuse of LLMs, Stack Overflow, etc) is that it's a false economy. If you're using your tools unsustainably, you might save labor early on, and you might even make something useful to others! But it could result in a rat's nest of code that someday won't fit in your LLM's context window, or whose bugginess will alienate all your users. Digging yourself out from that will cost more labor in the long run.

I think Claude assisted coding is still engineering, as long as an engineer is still making decisions and all code is reviewed. I use Claude myself and it has made me more productive on some tasks, especially smaller changes, but I’ve learned to pick and choose what I get it to do.

But that’s not vibecoding, which as I understand it is epitomised by Yegge’s comment that he’s “never seen the code”.

Frankly, I think it’s absolutely irresponsible to publish a product with code you’ve never read. My guess is that it’s all going to come crashing down on folks. Especially people who are pushing out production code based on this stuff.

LLMs are amazing technology, but the problem has never been writing the code, but understanding what needs to be done. If you spend just as much time writing English as you do writing code, I’m not sure what the benefit is.

I think you're saying that many problems with computing come from an attempt to fit requirements into "scientific" boxes, but that's not really my position - I certainly agree that requirements gathering is one of the hardest problems in computing, and possibly even somewhere that LLMs can help. But in any case, that's squishy social stuff that's also true in other engineering fields.

My position is more that software engineering - developing and deploying the actual code - is about applying principles from logic, discrete maths, computer science, etc to write code. Like, if you need to search for something, you can select from a number of algorithms with various O and constant time properties depending on the actual problem. That's what I think of as engineering, and that's the sort of analysis that LLMs don't seem to do very well.

text:
I always view new ideas from the PoV of good faith and optimism. My first reaction, even artificially, is usually "super cool" and then "why is this going to be a good thing?" And then I get more critical from there. I'm a default-from-positivity type of person. I think too many technologists are pessimistic or dismissive by default. As a way of disclaimer, I'm also someone who productively and happily uses AI in my everyday life, including coding.

Despite all of the above, I will not use Gas Town. I don't find it trustworthy (on its OWN code basis, not even considering what it does). Beads is filled with questionable unsafe code paths.

But, I'm still an optimist! So how does that apply here...

Well, I think all things come with nuance. I don't believe an idea like Gas Town is going to replace engineering at large in most forms (if any) in the next 5 years even.

But, things like Gas Town (also colloquially referred to more generally as slop engineering, Ralph loops, etc.) have their place. I would MUCH rather some engineer ship a PoC of a product or feature using slop like Gas Town in a day spending hundreds of dollars than even the same amount of time (but likely more) on a standard Silicon Valley engineering salary.

Or, another point of view: agent orchestration is a huge challenge right now even for well-constrained problems where agents do really well. I highly highly predict this will be solved by the end of the year by all the major agentic programming providers. Gas Town is a [Wild West] approach to agent orchestration. Note when I say "agent orchestration", I mean basically a controlled Ralph loop: human aided design followed by "paint the owl" distributed over multiple agentic sessions, with control points where the AI/human can reconverge to verify its on the right path, rinse and repeat.

And that's where the idea is exciting and worth looking at seriously. I'm not a fan of throwing out the baby with the bathwater, so to speak. You can find something you personally find awful and still study it, play devil's advocate, learn from it, and find portions of it you can appreciate.

I still won't use Gas Town. :)

Me too, with regards to the good faith and optimism. I relish the moments when I discover a cool new tool that I can try out! Being a Zig fanboy, I was waiting with baited breath for Ghostty to be available for me to try.

So when beads was dropped, I jumped in and started seeing good results with it. As I mentioned in the article it just doesn't gel with the way I like to work. I'm just not comfortable with deploying code sight unseen. If storing AI metadata in version control is the way, our code review tools need to get better. Perhaps there is a market for human focused code review tools that automatically hide the AI cruft that is not important, and is safe to ignore.

I am still worried about the "erosion of expertise" as I like to call it. Where will we be in 10-20 years if the only entities that understand the fundamentals of software are AI agents?
